claims.text: The initial material is in a high-temperature BCC state.
Phase stability is governed by competition between thermodynamic driving forces for phase separation and diffusion-related kinetic limitations.
Temperature-dependent diffusion rates of the constituent elements mediate the response to isothermal holding.
Competition between thermodynamic driving forces and diffusion kinetics influences BCC-phase stability.
At lower temperatures, thermodynamic driving forces will overcome kinetic limitations and cause phase separation.
Phase separation will produce secondary phases.
At high temperatures, the BCC phase is retained because kinetic limitations dominate.
Vacuum or an inert atmosphere will prevent oxidation during isothermal holding.
Isothermal holds at different temperatures below the initial high-temperature state can test the proposed phase-stability mechanism.
SEM or TEM and X-ray diffraction can be used to detect microstructural phase separation and identify phases.
Specific diffusion rates and thermodynamic driving forces are insufficiently known to predict a phase-separation temperature range precisely.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says kinetic limitations dominate at high temperature but are overcome at lower temperature. This gives an internally inverted or unexplained temperature dependence, because diffusion-related kinetic limitations would ordinarily become stronger rather than weaker as temperature decreases.
